title: Fruit
levelNote: Six tiers in one file. Fruit is the right first noun — every one of them is a picture a four year old already knows — and it carries all the way up, because ripe, seasonal and imported are adult words about the same apple.
goal: Name fruit, say which you like, buy some, and describe how it tastes.

reading.title: Saturday morning
reading.text:
On Saturday my grandmother goes to the market. She takes a big basket and she takes me.

She buys oranges, a melon, and a lot of cherries. I carry the cherries because they are light. She talks to every person at every stall.

We come home late. The basket is heavy and my grandmother is happy. We eat the cherries before lunch, all of them.

reading.title: Sweeter than a lemon
reading.text:
Children work out very early that a lemon is sour and a mango is sweet, and they work it out without being told. What takes longer is understanding that sweetness is not a fixed property of a fruit. The same mango, from the same tree, is sour in September and sweet in December.

This is why asking whether a fruit is good is the wrong question at a market. The better question is whether it is ripe, and the answer changes weekly. A ripe pear is softer than an unripe one, heavier for its size, and smells like a pear from a step away.

An unripe pear smells of nothing at all. That is the test, and it is free.

questions.q: What do children work out early?
options: How to choose a ripe pear

questions.q: What is the better question at a market?

reading.title: Bred for the journey
reading.text:
A supermarket tomato is the most quoted example, but the same story has been told about strawberries, peaches and almost every apple you can buy in February. The variety on the shelf was not chosen because it tastes better than the alternatives. It was chosen because it survives being picked green, boxed, chilled, driven for two days and stacked under a light, and still looks like something you would want to eat.

That is a real achievement, and it is not what most people think they are buying. Flavour in fruit develops on the plant, in the last few days, and it cannot be recovered afterwards. Ripening and softening are not the same process; a fruit picked early will go soft on a shelf without ever becoming sweet, which is why so much winter fruit has the texture of ripeness and none of the taste.

None of this makes imported fruit a swindle. It makes it a trade, and a reasonable one: abundance in January, at the cost of flavour. What is worth noticing is only that the trade was made on your behalf, by somebody choosing a cultivar decades ago, and that nothing on the label mentions it.

speaking.tip: ba-NA-na. The middle is the loud one.
Don't like: the t almost disappears. Don-like.
Do you becomes d'you. Say it fast.
Haven't got is one push: hav-nt-got.

speaking.text: A mango is sweeter than a lemon.
speaking.tip: Than is weak here. It rhymes with fun, not fan.
Rise at the end. It is a yes-or-no question.
Have you ever runs together: hav-yoo-EV-er.

speaking.tip: Both was are weak. Only picked and ready are strong.
